evidence.label: Bi-Lipschitz Coordinates at Regular Points of Noncollapsed RCD Spaces

headline: Claims bi-Lipschitz coordinate charts around every regular point of a noncollapsed RCD space.
scope: Noncollapsed RCD(K,n) spaces, with reference measure exactly n-dimensional Hausdorff measure, for every real K and integer n ≥ 2, at every regular point.
plain: An RCD space is a possibly rough space whose curvature is bounded below in an averaged sense. At a regular point, zooming in always shows flat n-dimensional space. The paper claims every such point has a neighborhood that maps onto a piece of flat space. The map stretches distances by at most a fixed factor. The factor depends only on the dimension, and there is no Lean check.
doesNot: This does not say the metric is smooth or Hölder continuous in these charts, and it does not cover collapsed spaces. It has no Lean check.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Jeff Cheeger and Tobias Colding, who asked about a bi-Lipschitz upgrade for Ricci limit spaces
scorecard.significanceWhy: It claims to settle a conjecture on coordinates at every regular point, improving bi-Hölder charts to bi-Lipschitz ones.

explanation:
Start with the surface of a cube. Near a point in the middle of an edge, two faces meet. Unfold them flat and you get a piece of the plane, with distances kept exactly. A circle of radius r around that point has length 2πr, about 6.283 r. A corner is different. Three faces meet there, with total angle 3 × 90 = 270 degrees. A circle of radius r around the corner has length (3/2)πr, about 4.712 r. Zoom in on the corner and you still see a cone, never a flat plane.

A point is regular if every zoom-in limit there is flat n-dimensional space[1]. The edge point is regular and the corner is not. The cube's surface is an example of an RCD space. That is a possibly rough space with Ricci curvature, an averaged form of bending, bounded below by a number K, defined through optimal transport. Noncollapsed means volume is measured by the natural n-dimensional volume, Hausdorff measure[2]. A bi-Lipschitz chart is a map onto a piece of flat space that stretches or shrinks distances by at most a fixed factor L.

What was known? Cheeger and Colding found manifold neighborhoods with bi-Hölder charts and asked about a bi-Lipschitz upgrade[3]. Bi-Hölder charts can distort distances by a power, not just a factor. Mondino and Naber covered almost every point by measurable bi-Lipschitz pieces, but not open neighborhoods of each point[4]. Kapovitch and Mondino put the regular set inside an open region with bi-Hölder charts[5]. Honda and Zhang recalled the bi-Lipschitz conjecture[6].

The paper claims that every regular point has an open neighborhood bi-Lipschitz to an open subset of flat n-space[7]. The distortion factor depends only on the dimension[8]. It covers every regular point, not just almost every point[9]. The obstacle is that the natural harmonic coordinates can degenerate as the scale shrinks[10]. The paper compensates in the space of coordinate values. It tracks how much stretching is needed, scale by scale, and shows the total error stays small[11].

How sure is this? There is no Lean check. A computer proof checker has not looked at any part of it. The proof controls infinitely many scales at once with delicate estimates. No specialist review of the paper has been published.
hypeCheck: Solid if the proof holds. There is no Lean check, and no specialist review is published.

glossary.meaning: A possibly rough space with Ricci curvature bounded below, defined through optimal transport, and with a Hilbert-space calculus.
The reference measure is exactly n-dimensional Hausdorff measure, so the space has full dimension n.
A point where every zoom-in limit is flat n-dimensional space.
A map that changes every distance by at most a fixed factor, up or down.
A map whose distance distortion is bounded by powers of the distance, a weaker control than bi-Lipschitz.
A function that equals its own average around each point, like a steady temperature.
A natural way to measure n-dimensional volume using only distances.
